A lexical analyzer uses the following rules to recognize tokens over the alphabet ${a,b,c}$.

 

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Rule 1}  \quad  \quad & aa^*  & \text{{return Token1;}}   \\
\text{Rule 2} \quad \quad & c(a \mid b)^*   & \text{{return Token2;}}   \\
\text{Rule 3} \quad  \quad & a b^* c   & \text{{return Token3;}}   \\
\text{Rule 4} \quad \quad & caa^*   & \text{{return Token4;}}   \\
\end{aligned}
$$

When using regular expressions to scan an input, we resolve conflicts by taking the largest possible match at any point. If two longest matches are of same length then we give preference in the below order : $\text{Rule 1 > Rule 2 > Rule 3 > Rule 4}$

Assume we have two graphs $\text{G}_1=\left(\text{V}_1, \text{E}_1\right)$ and $\text{G}_2=\left(\text{V}_2, \text{E}_2\right)$. Also assume that we have $\text{T}_1$ which is a MST of $\text{G}_1$ and $\text{T}_2$ which is MST of $\text{G}_2$. Now consider a new graph $\text{G = (V, E)}$ such that $V=\text{V}_1 \cup \text{V}_2$ and $E=\text{E}_1 \cup \text{E}_2 \cup \text{E}_3$ where $\text{E}_3$ is a new set of edges that all cross the cut $\left(\text{V}_1, \text{V}_2\right)$

Following is an example of what $\text{G}$ might look like. The dashed edges are $\text{E}_3$, the solid edges in $\text{G}_1$ (on the left) are $\text{T}_1$, and the solid edges in $\text{G}_2$ (on the right) are $\text{T}_2$.

Now assume we want to find a MST of the new graph $\text{G}$. Consider the following algorithm which tries to do this:

 

Algorithm:
Maybe-MST$(\left.\text{T}_1, \text{T}_2, \text{E}_3\right)$
{

  1. $\text{e}_{\min }=$ a minimum weight edge in $\text{E}_3$
  2. $\text{T}=\text{T}_1 \cup \text{T}_2 \cup\left\{\text{e}_{\min }\right\}$
  3. return $\text{T}$

}

If all edges in $\mathrm{G}_1$ and $\mathrm{G} 2$ has distinct weights then algorithm correctly finds out MST for $\text{G}$
Algorithm does not calculate MST for $\text{G}$ even if $\text{G}_1$ and $\text{G}_2$ are trees with distinct weights

Consider the C program fragment which uses a function $\text{foo}$.
 

main(){
    int *p = foo();
    p = NULL;
    //some other stuff
}


$\text{foo}$ can be implemented in various following ways, all pieces of code are identical except for their use of free(). Each of them may be correct or they may have a memory leak, dangling pointer or both.

$\textsf{P1:}$

int *copy(int *src) {
    int *dst = malloc(sizeof(int));
    *dst = *src;
    return dst;
}
int foo() {
    int a = 3;
    int *b = copy(&a);
    return * b;
}


$\textsf{P2:}$

int *copy(int *src) {
    int *dst = malloc(sizeof(int));
    *dst = *src;
    free (dst);
    return dst;
}
int foo() {
    int a = 3;
    int *b = copy( &a);
    return * b;
}


$\textsf{P3:}$

int *copy(int *src) {
    int *dst = malloc(sizeof(int));
    *dst = *src;
    return dst;
}
int foo() {
    int a = 3;
    int *b = copy( &a);
    free (b);
    return * b;
}

Which of the following is/are CORRECT?

You should provide an answer for the complete program, which includes combining the main function with a specific implementation of the function $\text{foo}$.

options.html: $\text{P2}$ does not have memory leak or dangling pointer
$\text{P3}$ does not have memory leak or dangling pointer

Ben Bitdiddle wants to implement a concurrent application. Instead of doing the sensible thing and holding a lock while manipulating shared data, Ben decides to be clever. while (i < 3) {
    while (i % 2 == 0);
    P(x_lock);
    x[i] = 1;
    i = i + 1;

}

while (i < 3) {
    while (i % 2 == 1);
    P(x_lock);
    x[i] = 2;
    i = i + 1;
    V(x_lock);
}

A system uses $2$ level page tables to implement virtual memory. Outermost page table has $32$ entries, each pointing to one page of the innermost page table. Outermost page table entry has a simple format : a valid bit followed by the Physical Frame Number of the page of the page table (if valid). If $w$ is a string over some alphabet $A$ then we say that $w$ has $|w|$ positions in it. Empty string has $0$ positions. For instance, the string $abaab$ has five positions, $1$ to $5,$ where position $1$ has symbol $a,$ position $5$ has symbol $b.$
For any string $w$, Let $\text{Q}(a, x)$ be a predicate defined as "symbol $a$ is at position $x$”, where $x$ ranges over the positions of $w$.

For instance, for a string $w \in\{a, b\}^*$, the property "all symbols are $a$" is formalized by the formula $\forall x \text{Q}(a, x)$. In order to express relations between positions we add to the syntax the predicate $x \lt y$, with intended meaning "position $x$ is smaller than (i.e. lies to the left of) position $y$".

Let $\text{L}$ be a language over the alphabet $\{a, b\}$ such that the strings in $\text{L}$ are described by the given expression: $\forall x(\text{Q}(a, x) \rightarrow \exists y(y\gt x \wedge \text{Q}(b, y)))$ where domain for the variables $x,y$ is the set of positions of the respective string. For instance, if $w=a a b a$ then domain for $x, y$ will be the set containing $1,2,3,4$. The number of states in the minimal DFA(Deterministic Finite Automaton) which accepts the language $\text{L}$ is ____________

A classical RISC five-stage pipeline is depicted below:

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline \begin{array}{c}
\text { instruction } \\
\text { fetch }
\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}
\text { register } \\
\text { fetch }
\end{array} & \text { execute } & \begin{array}{c}
\text { memory } \\
\text { access }
\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}
\text { register } \\
\text { write back }
\end{array} \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

The pipeline has the following characteristics.

  • The register file is written at the end of the clock cycle.
  • The pipeline does not have other bypassing/forwarding hardware.

Consider the following sequence of assembly instructions:

#1: ADD R1, R2, R3
#2: SUB R4, R1, R5
#3: AND R6, R1, R7
#4: OR R8, R1, R9
#5: XOR R10, R1, R11

In all the above instructions, the destination register is the first (leftmost) register.
A read-after-write(RAW) data dependency occurs when a later instruction requires an input value that is set by an earlier instruction. A RAW data hazard occurs when one instruction writes a value into a register that will be used as input by a later instruction, but that value does not actually appear in the register by the cycle on which the later instruction attempts to read it.
Note that a RAW data hazard always implies a RAW data dependency, but some RAW data dependencies do not imply a RAW data hazard.
Identify the data hazards that would prevent the given sequence of instructions from executing correctly on the given hardware design above, unless the compiler inserted one or more nop instructions for correct execution.
Which of the following statements is correct?

options.html: Every RAW dependency in the given program is a RAW data hazard for the given pipeline.
The number of RAW dependencies in the given program is $4$ but only $1$ of them is a RAW data hazard for the given pipeline.
The number of RAW dependencies in the given program is $4$ but only $3$ of them are  RAW data hazards for the given pipeline.
The number of RAW dependencies in the given program is $1$ and it is a RAW data hazard for the given pipeline.

questions.solution:
